Clergy work falls into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is ritual and teaching: praying and promoting spirituality, preparing and delivering sermons or other addresses, reciting scriptures (such as the Bible and the Torah and the Quran), organising and leading regular religious services, leading special ceremonies such as weddings and funerals and confirmations, administering religious rites or sacraments, and helping people prepare to take part in religious services. The second is companionship and counselling: providing counselling to individuals or groups on spiritual and emotional and personal needs, visiting homes and hospitals and prisons to offer comfort and support, responding to requests for help in emergencies or crises, and referring those in need to community support services and psychologists or doctors. The third is organisation and congregational management: training leaders of the church and community and youth groups, planning or leading religious education programmes, studying and interpreting religious law and doctrine and tradition, working with committees or individuals on the congregation's financial or administrative affairs, organising or taking part in interfaith and community and civic and educational or recreational activities, teaching believers about religious topics or writing articles or giving addresses, expanding the congregation, and taking on administrative duties such as building management or purchasing or contracting or supervising staff and volunteers, as well as taking part in fundraising.

Six recurring occupational judgements: whether the object and requirements of the ceremony are clearly confirmed; whether sermon and teaching content is faithful to the scripture and tradition it rests on; whether the boundaries of confidentiality and referral in visits and counselling are held; whether the protection of minors and crisis response follow procedure; whether congregational and financial and personnel matters are open and verifiable; and whether important communications and decisions leave an appropriate record.
Judgement one: are the object and requirements of the ceremony clearly confirmed

First confirm the type of ceremony and the participants and the venue and the time and the sacred objects and texts to be prepared, and check the wishes and taboos with the parties concerned; when in doubt, ask before arranging.
Judgement two: is the sermon and teaching content faithful to the scripture and tradition it rests on

Study the original texts and commentaries and congregational tradition, distinguish the original meaning of scripture from personal interpretation and state the basis in what you say; on doctrinal disagreements follow denominational procedure rather than a personal ruling.
Judgement three: are the boundaries of confidentiality and referral held

Keep spiritual care separate from psychological counselling and medical and legal matters; refer requests for help beyond your ability and duties to procedure and explain the scope and exceptions of confidentiality.
Judgement four: are the protection of minors and crisis response carried out to procedure

Editorial crisis note: when there is an urgent risk of self-harm, harm to others or abuse, protect people promptly under the actual plan and contact the appropriate emergency or professional services, without waiting to complete an internal report before seeking help; reporting duties and exceptions to confidentiality are checked against the applicable laws, the actual body and the duties, and you do not undertake diagnosis or treatment beyond your training and authority.
Judgement five: are congregational and financial and personnel matters open and verifiable

Confirm financial and purchasing and fundraising and personnel arrangements together with the committee or representatives of the congregation, and keep resolutions and accounts and contract records, avoiding acting alone.
Judgement six: do important communications and decisions leave an appropriate record

Write ceremony arrangements and visits and referrals and crisis handling and congregational resolutions into appropriate records so that, while privacy is protected, handover and review can be traced.

Clergy lead religious worship and perform other spiritual functions associated with beliefs and practices of a religious faith or denomination, providing members with spiritual and moral guidance and assistance; the typical closed loop is understanding the community's needs and preparing sermons and teaching, leading ceremonies and administering the corresponding rites, visiting and counselling those in need and referring as required, handling congregational and financial and personnel matters, and leaving appropriate records while protecting privacy.

paragraphs: The six directions share part of their skills with this occupation: building and maintaining relationships with people, listening and communicating, staying steady in a crisis, and leaving a record of the process. The real differences lie in the nature of the duties and the regulatory system: the clinical and therapy directions require regulated practice qualifications and carry responsibility for diagnosis and treatment, the counselling and social work directions require the corresponding professional training and organisational duties, the management direction is responsible for programmes and budgets and performance, while the core of this occupation is religious ceremony and teaching and spiritual companionship and responsibility for congregational affairs. When choosing, it is better to first validate with one deliverable ceremony and teaching preparation and visit record than to compare names.

items.title: What evidence employers usually look at

values: Prompt materials T1—T4 (fictional paper material)

T1 fictional non-religious management parable (not scripture or doctrine): A leaves two umbrellas at the door for neighbours to borrow. B borrows one and notes the return time on a slip of paper; C leaves a broken umbrella behind, and the manager first confirms the damage, then agrees the repair with the borrower. Note N1: the text states only the two umbrellas, the borrowing record and confirming before agreeing; everyone should help without payment is an added interpretation that the text cannot prove.

T2 fictional community: 12 adults attend a 20-minute indoor item mutual-aid briefing, the purpose being to explain the borrowing record and the maintenance boundary; the roles are facilitator P, recorder Q and safety contact R, the venue is only a paper assumption, and a budget of 300 yuan has internal approval and fundraising is not allowed.

T3 fictional adult A says I have not slept well since the bereavement, please diagnose me and advise me to stop the medication. The record contains only case number A, the exact words, and the willingness to listen and refer; there must be no diagnosis, no advice to stop medication and no promise of an outcome. Fictional resource M is a qualified medical service and S is a social support service, both with no real address or contact details, and no real referral is carried out.

T4 fictional safety situation: youth B mentions being harmed, and this is used only for a tabletop exercise. Fictional exercise procedure: identify the clue and flag it immediately to R; R contacts the assumed protection and emergency service channel, and Q records only the time, the clue and the handover, without investigating personally or promising absolute confidentiality; the paper handover is completed within 10 minutes and reviewed in writing the same day. These time limits are the scenario, not legal deadlines. The real reporting duty is checked against local law and the duties of the body.
Four submitted pieces of work
Piece 1: use T1/N1 to write a 10-minute non-religious explanatory outline, marking each section as source fact or editorial interpretation; no religious preaching.

Piece 2: based on T3, write a listening and referral plan including the exact words, a non-diagnostic response, asking about willingness, the exceptions to confidentiality and minimum necessary records.
Piece 3: based on T4, write a safety handover card (the clue, the R/Q duties, the scenario time limits, the paper record, the review), without rehearsing a real visit, contact or handling.

Piece 4: based on T2, write a 20-minute briefing checklist, the division of labour and a budget of no more than 300 yuan, recording approval and settlement; do not organise a real ceremony or activity.
Reference answers and review criteria

Reference piece 1: opening 1 minute; three source facts 3 minutes; explanation of borrowing and confirming first 2 minutes (marked as interpretation); one counter-example 2 minutes; summary and questions 2 minutes, 10 minutes in total. The text does not support everyone must help without payment, and it should be deleted or explicitly marked as an assumption.

Reference piece 2: record A's exact words; respond that you can listen but cannot diagnose or advise stopping medication; ask about willingness to contact M and offer the fictional S support lead; record only the necessary information and, if a safety clue appears, hand over to R as in the scenario, without promising absolute confidentiality.

Reference piece 3: receive B's clue → hand over to R immediately → Q records the time, a summary of the exact words and the person handed over to → complete the paper handover within 10 minutes → review the same day; do not investigate personally or leave B to carry the contact task alone. Real events cannot reuse the fictional roles and time limits.

Reference piece 4: opening 2 minutes, borrowing explanation 5, maintenance boundary 5, questions 5, handover 3, 20 in total; P facilitates, Q records the budget and receipts, R checks the paper safety; paper 50, item labels 100, contingency 150 = 300 yuan, with no real payment or fundraising.
Limits of the exercise
All of it is a fictional paper exercise that uses no real religious material, personal data or participants, is not published online, and does not use AI to proselytise.
The pieces only prove that the exercise was completed; they grant no religious office, ceremony leadership, psychological medical or legal service, or real crisis-handling qualification.
It practises only textual expression, boundary records and collaboration, and does not test religious doctrinal literacy or real ceremony skills.

Exercise evidence uses only the four fictional pieces T1—T4; if real work evidence is to be used, first check the lawful basis for processing, the authority and the sensitive information protection conditions, as de-identification alone is not enough.
For items with no evidence, mark them clearly as to be supplied and give a plan for supplying them.
Independent review
Review your own four fictional pieces: whether the source/interpretation, the 10 minutes, the 20 minutes, the budget, the minimum necessary records and the safety handover are complete.
Write the omissions and the basis into a revision table, and do not collect real visit material; de-identification alone does not automatically satisfy the information processing conditions.
